common_name: Lemon Squash (Vegetable Lemon, Heirloom Round Summer Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed past 65F, since this old American variety sulks in cold, wet ground the way most summer squash do.

directions: Lemon Squash has been grown in American gardens since the 1890s, prized for its round, pale yellow fruit that genuinely resembles a lemon in size and shape rather than a typical zucchini or crookneck. Pick fruit at 2-3 inches across for the sweetest, most tender eating, since the thin skin toughens and the flavor turns bland if left to balloon past baseball size. The sprawling bush produces steadily through summer heat, so check plants every day or two once fruiting begins to avoid a surprise crop of oversized squash. It can be used wherever a round summer squash is wanted — sliced, stuffed, or sauteed — and its unusual shape makes it a conversation piece at farmers markets.

common_name: Striato d'Italia Zucchini (Italian Heirloom Striped Zucchini)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed well past the last frost date, giving the semi-trailing vines ample room to spread.

directions: Striato d'Italia is a long-grown Italian market variety, its medium green skin broken by pale longitudinal stripes that run the length of the fruit, distinguishing it at a glance from the deeply ribbed Costata Romanesco. Harvest at 6-8 inches, before the stripes fade and the rind thickens, for the finest-textured flesh and the mildest flavor. The vines are more rangy than modern bush hybrids and benefit from occasional redirection so fruit doesn't hide and oversize under the leaves. It holds up well in classic Italian preparations such as frying in rounds or grilling, where its firm, less watery flesh is an advantage over standard green zucchini.

common_name: Long Green Trailing Marrow (Classic English Vining Vegetable Marrow)

planting.note: Direct sow after frost danger passes and give the vigorous trailing vines a generous bed or sturdy support, since this is a true running type rather than a compact bush.

directions: Long Green Trailing is one of the traditional English vegetable marrows, grown on long rambling vines rather than the compact bush habit of most modern zucchini. Gardeners can pick it young, at 8-10 inches, for a tender zucchini-like squash, or let it grow on toward 18-24 inches for the classic British marrow, which is typically halved, stuffed, and baked rather than eaten raw. Because the vines run rather than stay in a tidy mound, train them along a fence or let them ramble through an open bed to keep the dark green, pale-striped fruit easy to find. This old allotment favorite is prone to the same squash vine borer and powdery mildew pressures as other pepo squash, so monitor the sprawling stems through the season.

common_name: Verte Non Coureuse des Maraichers (French Heirloom Bush Zucchini)
scientific_name: Cucurbita pepo 'Verte Non Coureuse des Maraichers'

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed after the last frost; its compact bush habit suits smaller garden beds better than trailing marrow types.

directions: Verte Non Coureuse des Maraichers -- literally the market gardeners' 'green, non-running' squash -- was selected as a tidy bush zucchini for growers who needed productive plants without the sprawl of older trailing French varieties. Pick the dark green fruit young, around 6-7 inches, when the skin is still glossy and the seeds are barely formed, for the best texture in classic French preparations like ratatouille. Its compact habit makes it a good choice for raised beds or smaller kitchen gardens where trailing marrows would take over. Keep picking regularly, since like most bush zucchini it will quickly funnel energy into a few oversized fruit if left unharvested.

common_name: Patisson Panache Jaune et Vert (French Heirloom Striped Pattypan Squash)
scientific_name: Cucurbita pepo 'Patisson Panache Jaune et Vert'

planting.note: Direct sow once the soil is reliably warm after the last frost; scallop-type squash resents cold, soggy soil at germination.

directions: Patisson Panache Jaune et Vert is a traditional French scallop squash, its saucer-shaped fruit mottled in yellow and green rather than solid white, gold, or green like more common pattypans. Harvest small, at 2-3 inches across, when the rind is still soft enough to pierce with a fingernail, for a sweet, delicate squash best simply sauteed or steamed. Left on the vine, the fruit develops a harder rind and coarser flesh more suited to drying or ornamental use than fresh eating. Like other scallop types, it benefits from frequent picking to keep the compact bush setting new fruit through the season.

common_name: Table Dainty Marrow (Compact English Heirloom Vegetable Marrow)

planting.note: Direct sow after frost danger passes; its smaller bush habit suits allotments and raised beds better than the big trailing marrows.

directions: Table Dainty is a classic English bush marrow bred to stay smaller and more manageable than old-fashioned trailing marrows, producing pale green, lightly striped fruit on compact plants. Cut fruit young, around 6-8 inches, to eat it like a zucchini, or let it grow toward a modest 10-12 inches for a true marrow to halve, stuff, and bake. Its restrained size and bush habit make it a practical choice for smaller UK allotment plots where a full-sized trailing marrow would sprawl out of bounds. Pick regularly once fruiting starts, since even this compact variety will stop setting new fruit if a few are left to grow oversized.
